email-predictions.t: A spam filter has classified some emails. Here are **ten of them**; later we use all **100 emails** of the evaluation set. Our job is to count exactly how the filter is right and wrong.

actual-labels.t: Each email has an **actual class**: spam or legitimate. **Spam is our positive class**, the thing we are trying to find.

predicted-labels.t: The filter also gave each email a **predicted class**. Comparing actual with predicted shows where it was **right and where it was wrong**.

correct-spam.t: **Actual spam, predicted spam** is a **true positive (TP)**: the filter caught it. Three of these ten emails are TP.

missed-spam.t: **Actual spam, predicted legitimate** is a **false negative (FN)**. The filter **missed** this spam, and it reaches the inbox.

false-alarm.t: **Actual legitimate, predicted spam** is a **false positive (FP)**. A good email was **blocked by mistake**: a false alarm.

correct-legitimate.t: **Actual legitimate, predicted legitimate** is a **true negative (TN)**: a good email correctly allowed through.

build-matrix.t: The four outcomes go into a 2 × 2 table. **Rows are the actual class, columns are the predicted class.** We use this orientation everywhere in the course.

fill-counts.t: Over all 100 emails: **TP = 16, FN = 4, FP = 8, TN = 72**. The four counts add up to 100, so every email appears in exactly one cell.

read-matrix.t: Rows give the actual totals: **20 spam and 80 legitimate**. The diagonal (16 + 72 = 88) is correct, so accuracy is **0.88**. The off-diagonal cells show **which mistakes** were made, which accuracy alone hides.
